meta.generationSource: Our World in Data, "Electricity production by source" (Ember + Energy Institute Statistical Review + historical estimates), CC BY 4.0.
meta.subfuelSource: Eurostat nrg_bal_peh, gross electricity production by fuel. Sub-fuel shares are applied to the OWID parent total so the two sources reconcile.
meta.carbonSource: IPCC AR5 WGIII Annex III Table A.III.2 lifecycle medians (gCO2eq/kWh), read from the published PDF. Fuels absent from that table are derived and flagged.
meta.aiDisclosure: The application around this dataset was built by an AI system. The generation figures are ingested verbatim from published statistics and are not modelled; the carbon series is generation multiplied by a published emission factor.

entities.label: World
entities.note: Worldwide electricity generation. The series runs from 1900, when total world output was around 6 TWh — less than a mid-sized power station produces today — to more than 31,000 TWh. Coal has been the largest single source throughout, but the composition around it has changed completely: oil rose and fell, nuclear rose and plateaued, and wind and solar went from nothing to the fastest-growing sources in twenty years.

entities.label: European Union
entities.note: The European Union (27 members, on current boundaries). Notable for the earliest large-scale coal phase-out, a heavy nuclear component concentrated in France, and the most detailed public statistics of any major economy — Eurostat is the reason the coal, oil and bioenergy bands in this chart can be broken down by fuel type at all.

entities.label: United States
entities.note: The United States. Coal supplied over half of US electricity as recently as 2005 and has since fallen below 20%, displaced largely by natural gas following the shale boom rather than by renewables. The US nuclear fleet is the largest in the world by output despite almost no new construction since the 1970s.

entities.label: China
entities.note: China generates more electricity than any other country, more than the United States and European Union combined. Its output roughly quintupled between 2000 and 2024. Coal remains the backbone of the system, but China is simultaneously the largest builder of wind, solar, hydro and nuclear capacity in the world, so both the coal band and the renewables bands grow at once.

entities.label: India
entities.note: India is the third-largest electricity producer and among the fastest-growing. Its system is heavily coal-based, with domestic lignite and imported bituminous coal, and has added solar capacity rapidly since 2015. Per-capita consumption remains far below the OECD average, so demand growth is expected to continue for decades.

entities.label: United Kingdom
entities.note: The United Kingdom has the longest continuous record in this dataset, from 1920. It offers an unusually complete arc: near-total coal dependence into the 1960s, the "dash for gas" after privatisation in the 1990s, and one of the fastest coal exits of any major economy — the last coal-fired power station closed in September 2024.

entities.label: Germany
entities.note: Germany combines an early and large renewables build-out under the Energiewende with a nuclear phase-out completed in April 2023, and retains a substantial domestic lignite industry. It is the clearest example in this dataset of lignite's persistence: brown coal from domestic open-cast mines still generates more than hard coal.

entities.label: France
entities.note: France derives a larger share of its electricity from nuclear power than any other country, following a state-directed construction programme launched after the 1973 oil shock. The result is one of the lowest carbon intensities of any large grid, and a system whose principal vulnerability is correlated outages across a standardised fleet.

entities.label: Poland
entities.note: Poland has the most coal-dependent electricity system in the European Union, drawing on both domestic hard coal from Silesia and lignite. Its transition away from coal is among the slowest in the EU and is closely tied to regional employment.

entities.label: Czechia
entities.note: Czechia relies on domestic lignite and on nuclear power from Dukovany and Temelín. It is a consistent net exporter of electricity to its neighbours.

entities.label: Spain
entities.note: Spain has among the highest wind and solar shares of any large European system, and is the world's largest deployer of concentrated solar power. It closed most of its coal capacity between 2018 and 2021.

entities.label: Italy
entities.note: Italy abandoned nuclear power by referendum after Chernobyl and relies heavily on natural gas and on imported electricity, giving it comparatively high prices and a carbon intensity above the EU average.

entities.label: Netherlands
entities.note: The Netherlands built its power system around the Groningen gas field, the largest in Europe, and is now closing it because of induced earthquakes. Offshore wind is the principal replacement.

entities.label: Greece
entities.note: Greece historically depended on domestic lignite, which is being retired rapidly in favour of gas and solar.

entities.label: Japan
entities.note: Japan idled its entire nuclear fleet after the Fukushima Daiichi accident in March 2011, replacing that output almost entirely with imported gas and coal. The discontinuity is one of the sharpest visible in this dataset. Restarts have been partial and slow.

entities.label: Brazil
entities.note: Brazil has one of the least carbon-intensive large grids in the world, built on hydropower — including Itaipu, for decades the largest power station on Earth. Its principal exposure is drought, which forces gas and coal plants to run.

entities.label: Canada
entities.note: Canada's grid is predominantly hydroelectric, with large provincial differences: Quebec, British Columbia and Manitoba are almost entirely hydro, while Alberta and Saskatchewan remain fossil-dependent.

entities.label: Russia
entities.note: Russia relies on domestic natural gas, with substantial nuclear and hydro components. It is one of the largest electricity producers in the world and a significant exporter of both power and reactor technology.

entities.label: South Africa
entities.note: South Africa has one of the most coal-intensive electricity systems in the world, operated largely by the state utility Eskom, and has experienced sustained load-shedding since 2007 as its ageing fleet has become unreliable.

entities.label: Norway
entities.note: Norway generates almost all of its electricity from hydropower, giving it among the lowest carbon intensities recorded anywhere, and uses its reservoirs as a balancing resource for neighbouring systems.

entities.label: Australia
entities.note: Australia's grid was built on domestic black and brown coal. Rooftop solar has been adopted faster there than in any comparable country, and now supplies a significant fraction of daytime demand.

entities.label: South Korea
entities.note: South Korea combines a large nuclear fleet with imported coal and liquefied natural gas. It has almost no domestic fossil resources, so its system is unusually exposed to fuel import prices.

nodes.label: Fossil fuels
nodes.note: Electricity generated by burning coal, oil or natural gas. Fossil fuels have supplied the majority of the world's electricity in every year since generation began, though their share has fallen from roughly 65% in 2000 to under 60% today as wind and solar have scaled. Because combustion releases carbon dioxide directly, this group accounts for almost the entirety of the power sector's emissions.

nodes.label: Nuclear
nodes.note: Electricity from controlled nuclear fission, commercially from 1954 onward. Global nuclear output grew rapidly until the late 1980s, then plateaued: it has hovered between roughly 2,500 and 2,800 TWh a year since 2000 while total generation more than doubled, so its share of the mix has roughly halved. Operating emissions are zero; lifecycle emissions arise from construction, fuel enrichment and decommissioning.

nodes.label: Renewables
nodes.note: Hydropower, wind, solar, bioenergy, geothermal and marine sources. Hydropower has been a significant contributor since the earliest years of electrification and remained the largest renewable source until the 2020s. Wind and solar were negligible before 2000 and are now the fastest-growing sources of electricity in absolute terms.

nodes.label: Coal
nodes.note: Coal has generated more electricity than any other single source for essentially the whole history of the industry, and still does. Output has been broadly flat at around 10,000-10,500 TWh since the mid-2010s, as declines in Europe and North America have been offset by growth in China and India. It is also the most carbon-intensive source in wide use, at roughly 820 gCO2eq/kWh over its lifecycle.

carbon.src: Lifecycle: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Coal - PC. Direct: fitted fleet average.

nodes.label: Oil
nodes.note: Oil-fired generation peaked in the 1970s, when it briefly supplied around a fifth of world electricity, and collapsed after the 1973 and 1979 oil shocks made it uncompetitive against coal and nuclear. It now accounts for under 2% of global output and persists mainly in island grids, remote systems and countries with domestic crude production. Per kilowatt-hour it is comparable to or worse than coal.

carbon.src: Lifecycle derived from IPCC 2006 default HFO factor at 38% efficiency. Direct: fitted fleet average.

nodes.label: Natural gas
nodes.note: Natural gas grew from a minor fuel to roughly a fifth of world electricity, driven by the efficiency of the combined-cycle gas turbine, which reaches around 60% thermal efficiency against roughly 40% for a conventional coal plant. Its lifecycle intensity of about 490 gCO2eq/kWh is close to half that of coal, though upstream methane leakage is a significant and contested component of that figure.

carbon.src: Lifecycle: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Gas - Combined Cycle. Direct: fitted fleet average, above CCGT because the fleet includes open-cycle and older plant.

nodes.label: Nuclear
nodes.note: Nuclear generation expanded rapidly through the 1970s and 1980s, then stalled following the Three Mile Island (1979) and Chernobyl (1986) accidents and, later, Fukushima (2011), after which Japan idled its entire fleet and Germany accelerated its phase-out. Absolute output has been roughly flat for three decades. At around 12 gCO2eq/kWh it is among the least carbon-intensive sources measured.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Nuclear

nodes.label: Hydropower
nodes.note: Hydropower was one of the first sources used for large-scale generation and remains the largest single low-carbon source worldwide. Growth is now constrained by the limited number of remaining suitable sites in developed economies, and output varies year to year with rainfall. Its lifecycle median of 24 gCO2eq/kWh conceals an unusually wide range: reservoirs flooding vegetation in warm climates can emit substantial methane.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Hydropower

nodes.label: Wind
nodes.note: Wind generation was negligible before the 1990s. Costs fell sharply through the 2010s and it has since become one of the two fastest-growing sources of electricity in the world. At roughly 11 gCO2eq/kWh over its lifecycle it is comparable to nuclear; essentially all of that arises from manufacturing and installation rather than operation.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Wind onshore

nodes.label: Solar
nodes.note: Solar generation was under 1 TWh worldwide in 2000 and passed 2,000 TWh in the 2020s — the fastest scale-up of any electricity source in history. The great majority is photovoltaic rather than concentrated solar thermal. Lifecycle emissions are dominated by panel manufacturing, and have fallen as production has shifted to more efficient cells and cleaner grids.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, mean of Solar PV rooftop (41) and utility (48)

nodes.label: Bioenergy
nodes.note: Electricity from solid biomass, biogas and the renewable fraction of municipal waste. Bioenergy is classified as renewable because the carbon released was recently absorbed from the atmosphere, but it is not carbon-free: the IPCC lifecycle median of about 230 gCO2eq/kWh reflects cultivation, processing and transport, and the treatment of biogenic carbon as neutral is an accounting convention that remains contested.

carbon.src: Lifecycle: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Biomass - dedicated. Direct: zero, biogenic CO2 treated as neutral (the least-squares fit returned -26, i.e. indistinguishable from zero).

nodes.label: Other renewables
nodes.note: Geothermal, tidal, wave and other marine sources. Geothermal dominates the band and is significant in a small number of countries with suitable geology — Iceland, New Zealand, Kenya, the Philippines, Indonesia and parts of the United States. Marine generation remains negligible worldwide despite decades of demonstration projects.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Geothermal (dominant technology in this band)

nodes.label: Lignite (brown coal)
nodes.note: Lignite, or brown coal, is the lowest rank of coal: high in moisture, low in energy density and generally uneconomic to transport, so it is burned close to where it is mined. It is the most carbon-intensive fuel in common use, at roughly a quarter more CO2 per kilowatt-hour than hard coal. Germany, Poland, Czechia, Greece, Bulgaria and Türkiye are the principal European users.

carbon.src: AR5 coal median scaled by UNECE 2021 lignite/hard-coal direct ratio (1.256)

nodes.label: Other bituminous coal
nodes.note: Other bituminous coal is the workhorse steam coal of the power sector: a hard, high-rank coal with good energy density, traded internationally on a large scale. It accounts for the majority of coal-fired generation worldwide.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Coal - PC

nodes.label: Sub-bituminous coal
nodes.note: Sub-bituminous coal sits between lignite and bituminous coal in rank. It has lower sulphur content than many bituminous coals, which made it attractive under US air-quality regulation; Wyoming's Powder River Basin is the largest source.

carbon.src: Between hard coal and lignite; AR5 coal scaled on carbon content

nodes.label: Coking coal
nodes.note: Coking coal is produced primarily for steelmaking rather than power. Its appearance in electricity statistics generally reflects by-products and off-specification material burned in power plants attached to industrial sites.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Coal - PC

nodes.label: Anthracite
nodes.note: Anthracite is the highest rank of coal: hard, dense, and almost pure carbon. It is scarce, expensive, and largely reserved for metallurgical and heating uses, so it accounts for a very small share of electricity generation.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Coal - PC (anthracite has the highest carbon content but also the highest heating value)

nodes.label: Coke & manufactured gases
nodes.note: Coke oven gas, blast furnace gas and other manufactured gases recovered from industrial processes and burned for power, typically on integrated steelworks sites.

carbon.src: Inherited from coal

nodes.label: Coal — type not reported
nodes.note: Generation that the detailed statistics do not break down by fuel type. The Eurostat fuel-level series begins in 1990, so earlier years sit entirely in this band, as does any generation the detailed return does not classify.

carbon.src: Lifecycle: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Coal - PC. Direct: fitted fleet average.

nodes.label: Fuel oil
nodes.note: Heavy fuel oil, the residual fraction left after lighter products are refined out of crude. It is the traditional fuel of oil-fired steam power stations.

carbon.src: Inherited from oil

nodes.label: Gas oil & diesel
nodes.note: Gas oil and diesel, used mainly in reciprocating engines and open-cycle turbines for peaking plant, standby generation and small island grids.

carbon.src: IPCC 2006 default gas/diesel oil factor (74.1 tCO2/TJ) at 38% efficiency

nodes.label: Petroleum coke
nodes.note: Petroleum coke, a solid carbon residue of refining. It is cheap and energy dense but very high in carbon and sulphur, and is the most carbon-intensive fuel in this dataset per kilowatt-hour.

carbon.src: IPCC 2006 default petroleum coke factor (97.5 tCO2/TJ) at 38% efficiency

nodes.label: Refinery gas
nodes.note: Refinery gas, a light hydrocarbon by-product burned on refinery sites, usually in combined heat and power plant.

carbon.src: IPCC 2006 default refinery gas factor (57.6 tCO2/TJ) at 38% efficiency

nodes.label: Other oil products
nodes.note: Remaining petroleum products used for generation, including orimulsion, naphtha and unclassified residues.

carbon.src: Inherited from oil

nodes.label: Oil — type not reported
nodes.note: Generation that the detailed statistics do not break down by fuel type. The Eurostat fuel-level series begins in 1990, so earlier years sit entirely in this band, as does any generation the detailed return does not classify.

carbon.src: Lifecycle derived from IPCC 2006 default HFO factor at 38% efficiency. Direct: fitted fleet average.

nodes.label: Photovoltaic
nodes.note: Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight directly into electricity with no moving parts. Essentially all growth in solar generation since 2010 has been photovoltaic.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Solar PV

nodes.label: Solar thermal (CSP)
nodes.note: Concentrated solar power uses mirrors to focus sunlight and raise steam, and can store heat to generate after dark. It was expected in the 2000s to rival photovoltaics; falling panel prices left it a niche technology, deployed mainly in Spain, the United States, Morocco and China.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Concentrated Solar Power

nodes.label: Solar — type not reported
nodes.note: Generation that the detailed statistics do not break down by fuel type. The Eurostat fuel-level series begins in 1990, so earlier years sit entirely in this band, as does any generation the detailed return does not classify.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, mean of Solar PV rooftop (41) and utility (48)

nodes.label: Solid biofuels
nodes.note: Solid biofuels: wood chips, pellets, agricultural residues and black liquor from pulp mills. This is the largest component of bioenergy generation.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Biomass - dedicated

nodes.label: Biogases
nodes.note: Biogas from anaerobic digestion of manure, sewage and food waste, and landfill gas. Capturing and burning methane that would otherwise vent gives it a lower net intensity than solid biomass.

carbon.src: Biogas is lower than solid biomass; AR5 biomass range lower half

nodes.label: Renewable municipal waste
nodes.note: The biogenic fraction of municipal waste burned in energy-from-waste plants. The non-renewable fraction of the same waste stream is counted under fossil fuels in most statistical frameworks.

carbon.src: Inherited from bioenergy

nodes.label: Bioenergy — type not reported
nodes.note: Generation that the detailed statistics do not break down by fuel type. The Eurostat fuel-level series begins in 1990, so earlier years sit entirely in this band, as does any generation the detailed return does not classify.

carbon.src: Lifecycle: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Biomass - dedicated. Direct: zero, biogenic CO2 treated as neutral (the least-squares fit returned -26, i.e. indistinguishable from zero).

nodes.label: Geothermal
nodes.note: Geothermal plants tap heat from the Earth's crust. Output is steady rather than variable, which makes it valuable for baseload, but it is viable only where hot rock lies close enough to the surface.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Geothermal

nodes.label: Tide, wave & ocean
nodes.note: Tidal and wave generation. Despite a long history of prototypes, worldwide output remains under 1 TWh a year — the smallest band in this dataset.

carbon.src: No AR5 row; placed between wind offshore and hydro

nodes.label: Other renewables — type not reported
nodes.note: Generation that the detailed statistics do not break down by fuel type. The Eurostat fuel-level series begins in 1990, so earlier years sit entirely in this band, as does any generation the detailed return does not classify.

carbon.src: IPCC AR5 Annex III, Geothermal (dominant technology in this band)

events.title: The grid begins
events.text: World electricity generation is around 6 TWh — less than a single large power station produces today. Roughly 40% of it is hydroelectric; the rest is coal-fired.

events.title: Coal takes the lead
events.text: Thermal generation pulls decisively ahead of hydropower as central coal stations grow large enough to serve whole cities rather than single districts.

events.title: Hoover Dam
events.text: Completed on the Colorado River, and for two years the largest power station in the world. The 1930s are the decade of state-financed hydro at scale, in the United States and the Soviet Union alike.

events.title: First nuclear electricity on a grid
events.text: The Obninsk reactor near Moscow supplies 5 MW to the Soviet grid in June 1954. Britain's Calder Hall follows in 1956 as the first station to deliver nuclear power commercially at scale.

events.title: The oil-fired decade
events.text: Cheap crude makes oil a mainstream generating fuel. Oil-fired output climbs to a peak in the mid-1970s, when it supplies around a fifth of world electricity.

events.title: The oil shock ends oil power
events.text: The 1973 embargo and the 1979 price spike make oil-fired generation uneconomic. Its share collapses over the following two decades and never recovers; today it is under 2%.

events.title: France commits to nuclear
events.text: The Messmer plan responds to the oil shock by ordering a standardised reactor fleet. France ends up deriving a larger share of its electricity from nuclear power than any other country.

events.title: Three Mile Island
events.text: A partial meltdown in Pennsylvania. No new US reactor ordered after 1978 was completed for more than thirty years, and the growth curve of world nuclear output bends here.

events.title: Chernobyl
events.text: The accident at Reactor 4 halts nuclear expansion across much of Europe. Global nuclear output continues rising into the 1990s on plants already under construction, then plateaus and has stayed roughly flat ever since.

events.title: The dash for gas
events.text: Combined-cycle gas turbines reach around 60% thermal efficiency against roughly 40% for conventional coal plant. Cheap turbines and liberalised markets make gas the default new build across Europe and North America.

events.title: China's coal build-out
events.text: China joins the WTO and its electricity demand roughly quintuples over the next two decades. Almost all of the growth in world coal generation this century happens in Asia; coal output in Europe and North America falls over the same period.

events.title: Fukushima
events.text: Japan idles its entire nuclear fleet after the March 2011 accident and replaces the output almost entirely with imported gas and coal. Germany brings forward its own nuclear phase-out, completed in April 2023.

events.title: Solar becomes cheap
events.text: Module prices having fallen by roughly 90% over the previous decade, solar moves from subsidised niche to the cheapest source of new electricity in much of the world. World solar output passes 1,000 TWh in 2021 and 2,000 TWh in 2024.

events.title: Wind and solar pass a tenth of world electricity
events.text: Together they supply more than 10% of global generation for the first time. Both are now adding more output each year than any other source, though coal generation has not yet begun to fall in absolute terms.

events.title: Britain closes its last coal plant
events.text: Ratcliffe-on-Soar shuts in September 2024, ending 142 years of coal-fired generation in the country that started it. Coal supplied 97% of British electricity as recently as 1970.
